title: Freeze the gates, trace the water
allegory: An attribution graph is a map of a canal city on one afternoon: freeze every lock gate as it stood, and the water reaching each basin becomes a simple sum of what upstream basins sent, so you can draw the big flows as arrows, prune the trickles, and test the map by damming one basin.
map: freezing every lock gate as it stood that afternoon
freezing attention patterns and LayerNorm scales at their values on this prompt
named basins you can point at
transcoder latents at the positions where they fire
how much of one basin's water reaches another
an edge weight: the source's writing vector, carried through the frozen layers, dotted with the target's reading vector

damming a basin to see whether the town downstream runs dry

chapters.name: Via Texas or not?
chapters.note: the capital of the state containing Dallas is...

cap.1: Ask a model for 'the capital of the state containing Dallas' and it says Austin. Did it think 'Texas' on the way, or just memorise the phrase?
cap.2: Attribution graphs answer questions like this for one prompt: a map of which internal features caused which, from the input tokens up to the predicted word.
cap.3: Circuit Tracing (Ameisen, Lindsey et al., Anthropic, 2025) built readable end-to-end graphs; the companion paper showed Claude 3.5 Haiku doing genuine two-step inference, Dallas to Texas to Austin.

cap.1: Picture a city of canals on one afternoon. Freeze every lock gate as it stood, and you can measure how much water from each basin reaches every other.
cap.2: Freeze attention patterns and LayerNorm scales at their values on this prompt, swap MLPs for transcoders, and the model is close enough to linear that each feature's pull on a later one is a number.
cap.3: The local replacement model: frozen hook_pattern and hook_scale, transcoders for MLPs. Given fixed feature activations the residual stream is linear in node activations, so batched backward passes give every edge.

cap.1: An arrow's strength: what the source basin pours in, carried along the frozen canals, measured where the target drinks. With gates frozen, it's one number.
cap.2: Each node writes a direction into the residual stream and reads one out. compute_adjacency_matrix gets source-writes, carried through the frozen layers, dotted with target-reads, via batched backward passes.
cap.3: For MLPs, skip + (mlp_out − skip).detach() with skip = ln(resid_mid) @ W_skip: exact forward, linear backward. The adjacency matrix is lower-triangular, since a transformer has no backward edges.

chapters.name: Count every route
chapters.title: Toy graph: direct arrow to the answer, then total influence

cap.1: Dallas has no arrow straight to the answer, yet it matters a lot, through Texas. Adding up every route, not just direct arrows, is how the map gets pruned.
cap.2: Even with sparse latents there are far too many nodes to read. Rank nodes and edges by total influence on the output, summing routes of every length, and prune below a threshold. (Toy weights.)
cap.3: On the normalised adjacency A, influence = A + A² + A³ + … = (I − A)⁻¹ − I, and the series ends because A is nilpotent. Toy route: 0.8 × 0.7 × 0.9 = 0.504 along Dallas → Texas → say Austin → answer.

cap.1: The pruned map: Dallas features light Texas features; Texas plus a 'say a capital' group light 'say Austin'. Zero out the Texas group and the answer breaks.
cap.2: Section 4 swaps your from-scratch code for the circuit-tracer library to get this graph. Annotated supernodes include Dallas, Texas, Say a capital and Say Austin; Texas is the first hop.
cap.3: A graph is a hypothesis: zero-ablate a supernode, or swap in another state's features and watch the capital change. On the Biology of a Large Language Model reports this structure in Claude 3.5 Haiku.

chapters.name: Gate, not wall

left.title: freeze the attention output
lines: every edge stays at one position
no route from Dallas to the answer

chapters.verdict: Fix how far each gate is open, not whether water flows through it.

cap.1: Freeze the gates, don't brick up the canals. Block the water itself and nothing crosses between streets, so no route from 'Dallas' to the answer can appear.
cap.2: Freeze the whole attention output and cross-position influence is zero everywhere: the graph splits into per-token islands. Freeze only hook_pattern and keep V @ W_O differentiable.
cap.3: Check before building: lower-triangular, non-zero embedding-to-first-layer entries, and average L0 per layer. Above 50 means you loaded the l0_big transcoders instead of l0_small, and nodes explode.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: A causal map for one prompt
A graph is a hypothesis: ablate to test it
Error nodes show what you missed

cap.1: To steer a model you need to know which of its ideas cause which. An attribution graph draws that map for one prompt, and ablations check it's true.
cap.2: It's activation patching and direct logit attribution generalised: compute all the edges at once, prune, then test. Graphs revealed two-step inference and rhyme planning in Claude 3.5 Haiku.
cap.3: Completeness, the share of input edges from features and embeddings rather than error nodes, says how much computation you captured. Anthropic's cross-layer transcoders shorten paths further.

coda.title: Toy graph: each node's total influence on 'Austin', after pruning

readouts.label: Dallas: direct arrow to the answer
does Dallas → Texas → Austin survive?
readouts.f: a*b*0.9 >= tau && b*0.9 >= tau ? 'yes' : 'no: pruned away'

caption.1: Raise the prune line and the stray feature goes first. Then weaken Dallas → Texas and watch the whole route vanish, even though 'say Austin' still stands.
caption.2: Total influence multiplies along a route and adds across routes. Pruning keeps nodes whose total clears the line, so one weak first hop can prune a whole chain. (Toy weights.)
caption.3: Here Dallas's influence is a·b·0.9, the single route Dallas → Texas → say Austin → logit. Real pruning thresholds both node and edge influence from the Neumann series on the normalised adjacency.

where_else: Activation patching and direct logit attribution: the one-hypothesis-at-a-time methods this generalises
Backprop: the same gradients, collected edge by edge between features instead of summed into weight updates
Hand-traced circuits like IOI in GPT-2: the same kind of map, drawn by hand
Supply-chain tracing: add up contributions along every route, then keep the big ones

hamming.what: A map of which internal features caused which on one prompt, built by freezing the model's messiest parts so every feature-to-feature influence is a number, then pruned to what matters.
hamming.when: When you want to know how a model reached a specific answer, like whether it really went Dallas to Texas to Austin, and you have transcoders for its MLPs.
hamming.why: It computes every edge at once instead of testing one hypothesis at a time, giving a readable causal map you can check by ablation.

object.title: The canal map
object.subtitle: Height is depth in the model; arrows are the strong influences left after pruning.

cap.1: The pruned graph for one prompt. Low nodes sit early in the model, high ones late; pulses show influence flowing up towards the answer.
cap.2: Input nodes are token embeddings, the middle are transcoder latents, the top is the predicted token. Only edges that survived pruning are drawn.
cap.3: A DAG over one prompt: embeddings, transcoder latents at firing positions, MLP error nodes and salient logits, with edges from the linearised model.

cap.1: From the front, the two-hop route stands out: Dallas up to Texas, Texas up to 'say Austin'. A separate 'say a capital' group joins at the top.
cap.2: The graph's claim: the model computes the state first, then combines it with a generic 'say a capital' signal to produce Austin.
cap.3: Two-step inference made visible: Texas is the intermediate hop, a claim you can only make with a graph you can intervene on.

cap.1: From the side, a grey error node: the part of an MLP the transcoder couldn't explain. The more arrows start there, the less the map captures.
cap.2: Error nodes carry each MLP's unexplained output. How much of the graph rests on them is your completeness check.
cap.3: Graph completeness is the fraction of input edges from feature and embedding nodes rather than error nodes.

cap.1: From above, every arrow points one way: up. A transformer has no backward edges, which is why adding up every route comes to an end.
cap.2: The adjacency matrix is lower-triangular, so summing routes of every length terminates.
cap.3: Nilpotent adjacency: Aᵏ = 0 beyond the longest path, so the Neumann series for total influence is a finite sum.

cap.1: Up close on Texas: the map claims this group carries the answer. Zero it out, or swap in another state's features, and the output should follow.
cap.2: Test the graph: zero-ablate the Texas supernode and the answer breaks; swap in another state's features and the model names that state's capital.
cap.3: Edges describe the replacement model; ablations and feature swaps check that the claim holds for the real model's output.

predict.q: Your graph only has edges within each token position. What did you freeze?

options.t: The whole attention output, not just the pattern

predict.why: Attention moves information between positions through V @ W_O. Freeze only hook_pattern and keep the value path differentiable.

predict.q: Dallas has no direct edge to the answer. Can pruning still keep it?

options.t: Yes: its influence flows through Texas

predict.why: Pruning uses total influence summed over every route via the Neumann series, not just direct edges.

predict.q: How do you check the graph's claim that the model goes via Texas?

options.t: Zero-ablate the Texas supernode and watch the answer

predict.why: A graph is a hypothesis. Ablating Texas breaks the answer, and swapping in another state's features changes it.

object.where: Anywhere you trace credit through a network of near-linear steps: spreadsheet dependencies, supply chains, citation graphs.
